extracted.intended_audience: historians, students, and general readers interested in the history of advertising, lotteries, and 18th-century British regulatory practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the regulatory standards, procedural rules, and advertising practices governing lotteries and lottery-insurance in 17th–18th century Britain as described in a history-of-advertising text. Focuses on statutory provisions, administrative procedures, penalties, and common advertising/fraud practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of private lotteries (10 & 11 William III c.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Act of Parliament (10 & 11 William III c.17) was passed for suppressing private or fallacious lotteries, even if they were set up under colour of patents or grants under the Great Seal; such grants/patents were declared void and against law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble states these grants 'are against the common good, welfare, and peace of the kingdom.' Penalties provided by the Act included £500 on proprietors of such lotteries and £20 on every adventurer in them. The Act was used to try to suppress private fraudulent lotteries despite continued evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering lottery tickets declared felony
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers gave notice that tickets which had been altered from blanks to numbers (i.e., fraudulent alterations) were detected and such alteration was declared a felony by the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The managers' public notices announced detection of altered tickets and explicitly warned that altering blanks to numbers constituted felony; this administrative declaration supported criminal prosecution of such tampering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize payment terms (pay at Bank in 40 days, without deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lottery schemes publicly stated payment terms for prizes: e.g., 'The Prizes to be paid at the Bank in 40 Days after Drawing, without Deduction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize schedules and payment guarantees were advertised as part of the scheme (showing transparency of payment timing and that payments would be made gross, without deductions), presumably to reassure subscribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resale limit for ticket delivery agents (no more than 20 to one person)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent monopoly of tickets and consequent price inflation, it was enacted that persons charged with the delivery of tickets should not sell more than twenty to one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision aimed at preventing concentration/monopoly by a few purchasers. In practice it was evaded (e.g., through use of fictitious 'lists'), undermining the protection and prompting later inquiries and prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited conduct by ticket receivers (early subscriptions, fictitious names, improper disposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific prohibited practices identified in prosecutions (e.g., Peter Leheup): (1) receiving subscriptions before the day and hour advertised; (2) permitting subscribers to use different/fictitious names to cover an excess of twenty tickets; (3) disposing of tickets which had been bespoke, not claimed, or double-charged instead of returning them to the managers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three violations were treated as breaches of trust and of the lottery Act; Leheup was prosecuted, found guilty, and fined (example fine £1,000). The entries show administrative rules around subscriptions and enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgery/counterfeiting of tickets and fabrication of winning numbers severely punished
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabricating winning numbers or counterfeiting lottery tickets was prosecuted as forgery/fraud; detected utterers and forgers were tried (in some cases together) and historically could be condemned to death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 1777 two men were examined for counterfeiting a winning ticket; other cases at the Old Bailey led to conviction and condemnation. The text notes that utterers of fabricated winning numbers were tried and punished alongside forgers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of detailed scheme (ticket count, price, prize schedule, blanks/odds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lottery advertisements/schemes publicly disclosed number of tickets, ticket price, detailed prize schedule, counts of blanks, and explicit notes on odds (e.g., 'little more than Three Blanks to a Prize').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemes and advertisements typically listed prizes, quantities, and payment conditions; such disclosures were used to attract subscribers and to present the odds and apparent fairness of the draw (even when the economics were against the buyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates exchange and office procedural notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers appointed by Act issued formal notices about administrative procedures: certificates for tickets entered at an office would be delivered at specified days/times and business (e.g., taking in tickets) could be suspended on specified dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural announcements governed how and where tickets were exchanged for certificates and gave public notice of administrative timelines; they also warned of detection and legal consequences for tampering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lottery advertising as puffery/news insertion to attract gullible subscribers
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters consistently used 'puffs' and pompous paragraphs—often inserted as ordinary news in newspapers—to stimulate speculation and trap gulls into subscribing to lotteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples (e.g., Post-Boy notices) and commentary on how these puffs generated public eagerness. This is presented as an advertising technique and an anti-pattern for ethical promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lottery-insurance offices claiming to guarantee special numbers (ostensible protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance offices were established that ostensibly guaranteed special numbers (supposedly protecting buyers and preventing fraud by sellers), acting as a form of insurance for ticket-holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although begun as a protection against certain abuses (e.g., sellers selling the same fractional ticket twice), these insurance offices 'in time became greater swindles than those they were supposed to prevent'—a caution about intermediary assurances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official commissioner's declarations and importance of drawing integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Official proclamations by lottery commissioners determined which tickets were declared prizes (example: a last-drawn ticket printed as entitled to £1,000 by commissioners' order, later complicated when another ticket was found lodged in the wheel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The episode highlights the reliance on official announcements and the need for transparency/integrity in the drawing process; disputes over wheel procedure and unexpected discoveries could cause public outcry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary oversight and sanctions for large-scale lottery fraud/complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament investigated and suppressed egregious lottery schemes (e.g., Hamburgh Lottery suppressed by special Act); members of Parliament and persons of rank implicated in lottery frauds could be expelled from the House and have property attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include expulsion of Viscount Barrington and others; Parliament used inquiries, reports, prosecutions, special Acts, and the imposition of remedies (such as instituting lotteries to compensate victims) as enforcement and remediation tools.
